passages.text: Exercise training combined with a high-fat diet improves the flesh flavour, texture and nutrition of gibel carp (Carassius auratus gibelio)
Highlights
A high-fat diet (HFD) increased muscle fat content but reduced flesh hardness.
Exercise training (ET) improved texture but reduced flavour amino acid contents.
Feeding a HFD restored flavour amino acid contents in fish flesh during ET.
ET combined with a HFD improved the flavour, nutritional value and aroma of flesh.

To meet the consumer demand for high-quality flesh sources, this study investigated the impacts of exercise training (ET) combined with a high-fat diet (HFD) on flesh quality. The results showed that HFD increased muscular fat content but reduced hardness, flexibility and adhesiveness. ET decreased fat content but increased flesh water holding capacity, hardness and stickiness. In terms of flavour, ET decreased the umami and sweet amino acid contents, which were restored when concomitantly feeding the HFD. Metabolomics further revealed that ET and HFD mainly affect the alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism, the citrate cycle and purine metabolism. The E-nose and volatile metabolomics analysis demonstrated that the combination of ET and HFD improved the aroma of flesh by enhancing the content of key flavour compounds within flesh such as hexadecenoic acid, ethyl ester and methyl stearate. This research provides a new strategy for improving the flesh quality of cultured fish.
Introduction

In recent years, as the global economy has continuously expanded and increased, consumer demands for food quality have increased. However, intensive farming patterns and the use of artificial compound feed have resulted in a deterioration in fish quality. The decline in meat quality could not only cause huge economic losses but also introduce meat safety problems. Therefore, improving fish quality is an urgent issue that must be addressed. Gibel carp (Carassius auratus gibelio) is a freshwater fish species that is widely cultured in Southeast Asia. According to reports, the production of gibel carp reached 2.7 million tons in China in 2020. Fish flesh quality is an important factor affecting consumers' willingness to purchase. This study explores potential strategies to improve the flesh quality of gibel carp with a view to enhancing its market value.

Dietary lipid content affects not only the physiological health but also the flesh quality of fish. Accumulating studies have indicated a positive correlation between dietary fat levels and intermuscular lipid levels in farmed fish. Fish flesh is the main source of polyunsaturated fatty acids and farmed fish fed high-fat diets are beneficial for humans to obtain more unsaturated acids. In addition, the sensorial quality of fish flesh is affected by intermuscular lipid content, particularly in terms of taste and texture. Fillets rich in fat possess a fatty and juicy flavour. However, excessive muscle fat has a negative impact on fillets. Currently, farmed fish have been partly fed a HFD to accelerate growth for greater economic benefits. However, high-fat feed causes a large accumulation of fat in fish bodies which not only affects the health of the fish but also reduces its flesh quality. Therefore, there is an urgent need to improve the quality of farmed fish without reducing farming profitability.

The quality of fish is affected by various factors, such as water temperature, rearing conditions, pre- and postslaughter handling and storage methods. In particular, an important factor in the quality of farmed fish is whether the fish performed exercise training prior to being slaughtered. To date, many studies have examined how swimming exercises alter meat quality indicators in fish. A previous study showed that swimming exercises could improve the muscular protein content in fish. Some remarkable differences in white muscle cellularity were observed between fish that perform exercise and fish that do not exercise. Exercising is an energy-burning process in which fish utilize more fuel to compensate for the increased energy expenditure during exercise. Thus, exercise has a nonnegligible impact on the pattern of chemical composition in the flesh and whole body of fish. Exercise training seems to be a potential measure for improving the quality of cultivable fish.

Volatile substances directly affect the preferences and choices of consumers, as these factors are an important feature of the perception of meat quality by consumers. When fish are cooked, the volatile substances in the flesh stimulate the appetite of individuals through the Maillard reaction. The volatile compounds are mainly composed of aldehydes, alcohols and lipids. Volatile compounds in fish can be produced by lipid oxidation, enzymatic reactions and microbial action. In addition, compounds can be developed as a result of environmental factors. At present, studies on the volatile compounds in fish flesh are mostly limited to different processing methods and storage treatments. The prelife feeding choices and activities of farmed fish have a strong impact on the type and amounts of volatile compounds in fish flesh. However, few studies have investigated the impacts of HFD and ET on the volatile compounds in fish flesh.

In the present study, the nutritional composition, texture, nonvolatile taste substances and volatile compounds in the flesh of gibel carp were analyzed qualitatively and quantitatively. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC/MS), ultrahigh-performance liquid chromatography coupled with high-resolution mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), texture analyzer and electronic nose (E-nose) analysis were performed jointly to comprehensively investigate the impacts of ET combined with HFD on the quality of fish flesh. This study provides a theoretical basis for improving the flesh quality of aquatic products.
Materials and methods
Experimental diets and animals

The formulation and chemical composition of the two experimental diets are shown in Table S1. All ingredients of diets were mixed and ground to a particle size of 100 mesh and then extruded using a win-screwed extruder (Jinan Dingrun Machinery Co., Ltd., Jinan, Shandong, China). The pellets were dried in an oven at 60  C and then stored at 4  C.

Gibel carp were purchased from the Guanqiao hatchery of the Institute of Hydrobiology, Chinese Academy of Sciences (Wuhan, Hubei, China). The experimental fish were acclimated for four weeks in fiberglass tanks (883 L water volume; 150 cm in diameter; 50 cm water depth) to adapt to the laboratory conditions. During the acclimation period, all fish were fed commercial feed twice a day. All experimental animal care protocols were approved by the ethics committee of the Institute of Hydrobiology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (IHB, CAS, Protocol No. 2016-018).
Feeding trial and exercise training

After acclimatization, healthy fish with similar size and body weight (initial weight 82.63 +- 0.16 g) were randomly distributed into two groups. Three tanks were randomly selected for each treatment. The fish in the two treatments were fed a medium-fat diet (7% fat) or a high-fat diet (13% fat). The two groups were set as the medium-fat diet (MFD) and high-fat diet (HFD) groups. During the feeding trial, the fish were fed to apparent satiation three times per day (8:30, 13:00 and 17:00) for 8 weeks. Water temperature was recorded daily and maintained at 30.05 +- 1.60  C. The dissolved oxygen content was maintained above 7.5 mg L-1 and the ammonia nitrogen content was<0.5 mg L-1. The photoperiod was 12 h light:12 h dark with a light period from 8:00 to 20:00. At the end of the feeding trial, the experimental fish from each treatment were divided into the following groups: a medium-fat diet, no exercise training group (MFN); a medium-fat diet, exercise training group (MFT), a high-fat diet, no exercise training group (HFN), and a high-fat diet, exercise training group (HFT). The fish in the no ET (N-ET) group swam at a water velocity of 2.5 cm s-1. In the ET group, the water flow was 16 cm s-1 (approximately 1.2 body lengths per second), which was induced with a water pump. The water pump functioned during 9:00-11:00, 14:00-16:00, and 18:00-20:00. During the exercise trains, the fish were fed to apparent satiation three times per day (8:30, 13:00 and 17:00) for 3 weeks. Other environmental conditions were the same as those in the feeding trial described above.
Sampling

After a short three-week exercise training experiment, the fish in all groups were weighed after being deprived of food for 24 h. 6 fish from each treatment were sacrificed by anesthetization with MS-222 (100 mg L-1 tricaine methane sulfonate, Argent Chemical Laboratories Inc., Redmond, WA, USA). All dorsal muscles were sampled and stored at -80  C until analysis. The dorsal muscle was dissected from another 3 fish from each treatment for texture analysis.
Flesh nutritional component analysis
Proximate composition analysis

The proximate compositions (moisture, ash, crude protein, crude, lipid and glycogen) of dorsal flesh samples and diets were performed following the method of the Association of Official Analytical Chemists. The specific detailed procedure was described in previous work.
Amino acid analysis

Hydrolyzed amino acids were determined by an amino acid analyzer (A300, MembraPure GmbH, Germany). Briefly, 50 mg of freeze-dried muscle was weighed and digested in 6 N HCl for 24 h at 110  C. The hydrolyzed sample was filtered and fixed into a 50 mL volumetric flask. One milliliter of fixed volume sample was aspirated into a brown bottle and placed it on a nitrogen blower to blow dry and deacidify at 60  C. Then, 1 mL deionized water was added into brown bottle and filtered through a 0.22 mum membrane. Finally, 20 muL of the solution was used to test hydrolyzed amino acids of flesh by an amino acid analyzer.

The methods of separating free amino acids from muscle were performed according to. The free amino acid levels in the dorsal muscle of fish were determined with the amino acid analyzer mentioned above.
Fatty acid analysis

The fatty acid compositions of dorsal muscle were determined according to the methods described by. The total lipids in the muscle samples were extracted using chloroform/methanol (V/V, 2:1) and then subjected to transesterification with methanolic sulfate to obtain fatty acid methylesters (FAMEs).
Flesh texture analysis
Flesh histological analysis

To understand the effects of diet and ET on the muscle histology of experimental fish, the muscle tissues from gibel carp were examined using H&E, PAS and Masson staining. This staining was performed by Servicebio Company (Wuhan, China). Thus, the morphology of flesh became visible. Muscle images (5 images sample-1) were captured from each slide using a fully automatic digital slide scanner (Aperio VERSA 8, Leica, Germany). ImageJ pro launcher software was used to identify myofiber characteristics, collagen and glycogen in dorsal muscle. In H&E sections, myofiber density was determined by the area of myofiber cross sections within a certain field. Myofiber diameter was calculated by examining a minimum of 20 fibers. In Masson and PAS sections, collagen and glycogen are colored blue and purple, respectively. The area of collagen and glycogen staining was quantified. The quantification of the above sections was completed by ImageJ pro launcher software.
Flesh texture profile analysis

A texture analyzer (Stable Micro systems, Ltd., UK) was used to determine the textural parameters of springiness, toughness, adhesiveness, stringiness, fracturability, stickiness and flexibility. The instrumentation procedure was based on the study by. Briefly, a 0.5 cm diameter spherical probe was used to press down on the flesh sample at a rate of 30 mm/min to give a deformation of 10 mm and the probe remained stationary in this position for 32 s. The springiness of flesh was obtained. The same probe applied a force of 2 N to the flesh sample, the load was held for 10 s and then the sample was left at a speed of 600 mm min-1. The toughness, adhesiveness, stringiness, fracturability, stickiness and flexibility were obtained. The centrifugal water loss expressed the water-holding capacity of the flesh, which was measured following the method elaborated by.
Analysis of nonvolatile taste substances
Determination of nucleotide and purine metabolite concentrations

The nucleotide and purine metabolite contents in flesh were measured according to a method previously described by with some modifications. Briefly, flesh samples (5 g) were minced and homogenized for 15 min in 10 mL of 0.1 M perchloric acid at 4 C. After centrifugation, the supernatant was neutralized with 1 M potassium hydroxide solution to a pH value of 6.4. The solution was diluted to 50 mL and filtered through a 0.45-mum Millipore syringe filter. A 20-muL aliquot of the filtrate was harvested and analyzed by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC, Waters 2695e, USA). The conditions for determining the content of nucleotides (inosine monophosphate (IMP), adenosine monophosphate (AMP) and adenosine diphosphate (ADP)) were as follows: a 5-mum C18 column (CNW Athena C18-WP, 4.6*250 mm, 5 mum). Mobile phase A, 0.01 mol L-1 potassium (KH2PO4); mobile phase B, methanol; column temperature, 30 C; flow rate, 1.0 mL min-1; injection volume, 20 microL; and UV detector wavelength, 254 nm. The conditions for the quantification of guanosine monophosphate (GMP), inosine, adenosine, hypoxanthine, adenine, guanine and xanthine concentrations were the same as described above except that 0.4753 g of the ion-pairing reagent tetrabutylammonium hydrogen sulfate (C16H37NO4S) was added to each liter of mobile phase A. The eluent compositions, gradient and HPLC program are presented in Tables S2 and S3.
Determination of the free amino acid composition
Free amino acid compositions were measured as described in section 2.4.2.
Extraction and determination of volatile compounds

2 g of fresh muscle sample was ground to a powder in liquid nitrogen, 1 g of the powder was transferred to a 20 mL head-space vial (Agilent, Palo Alto, CA, USA) and crimp-top caps with TFE-silicone headspace septa (Agilent) were used to seal the vials. At the time of headspace solid phase microextraction (HS-SPEM), each vital was placed in 100 C for 5 min. The volatile compounds from the sample were adsorbed using a 120 microm divinylbenzene/carboxen/polydimethylsilioxan fiber (Supelco, Bellefonte, PA, USA) for 15 min at 100 C. Finally, the volatile compounds were subsequently desorbed at 250 C for 5 min for GC/MS analysis. An Agilent Model 8890 GC and a 5977B mass spectrometer (Agilent), equipped with a 30 m x 0.25 mm x 0.25 mum DB-5MS (5% phenyl-polymethylsiloxane) capillary column were used to identify and determine the volatile compounds. Helium was utilized as the carrier gas at a velocity of 1.0 mL min. The temperature program for the oven was as follows: 40 C for 3.5 min, increase at 10 C min-1 to 100 C, increase at 7 C min-1 to 180 C, increase at 2 5C min-1 to 280 C and hold for 5 min. Mass spectra were recorded in electron impact (EI) ionization mode at 70 eV. The quadrupole mass detector, ion source and transfer line temperatures were set at 150, 230 and 280 C, respectively. Mass spectra were scanned in the range m z-1 50-500 amu with an interval of 1 s. The volatile compounds were identified by comparing the mass spectra with the data system library (NIST) and linear retention index.
Extraction and determination of nonvolatile compounds
The extraction and determination of nonvolatile compounds are performed by metabolomics. The specific methods are described in.
Electronic nose analysis

The odor profile of flesh (raw and cooked) from different experimental treatments was differentiated using an AIRSENSE Analytics GmbH Portable Electronic Nose (E-nose PEN3, Germany). The sensors and corresponding representative sensitive compounds of the E-nose are shown in Table S4. 2 g of homogenized sample (dorsal muscle of gibel carp) was placed in a 10 mL headspace vial, and the vial was sealed. After balancing at room temperature for 5 min, the gas in the headspace vial entered the sensor chamber through the injection needle at a speed of 400 mL/min. The intensities of 10 metal oxide sensors were measured and reported. The data acquisition lasted for 60 s and activated carbon filtered air was used to clean the sensing chamber and piping before each sample measurement. Another 2 g of dorsal flesh from the same sample was placed in a water bath and cooked at 70 C for 30 min. The cooked flesh was transferred into a headspace vial and balanced for 5 min. The subsequent steps were the same as above. For each part, eight parallel samples from each treatment were prepared for testing under the same conditions.
Statistics, calculation and visualization analysis

Two-way ANOVA analysis was first used to detect the possible interaction between ET and the dietary lipid level. If there was no interaction between the two factors. Under the same conditions (exercise training or no exercise training), an independent samples t test was used to analyze whether there was a significant difference between fish fed diets with different fat contents. Similarly, under the same dietary fat content (medium-fat diet or high-fat diet), the independent samples t-test was used to analyze whether there was a significant difference between fish at exercise training and no exercise training). All data are shown as the means with standard errors and differences were regarded as significant at P < 0.05.

The taste active value (TAV) was given by the following formulation: TAV = C/T, where C is the taste compound concentration (mg/100 g) and T is presented as the threshold value (mg/100 g). In general, the compounds in which TAV > 1 were considered flavour contributors.

The influence of dietary lipid level and ET on muscular volatile compounds was statistically analyzed using heatmap and principal component analysis (PCA). All data were processed and normalized by MetaboAnalyst 5.0, and then the differences in the levels of volatile compounds in muscle were analyzed.

For the E-nose data, principal component analysis (PCA) and an unsupervised method were used to visualize the data and detect the treatments in the data structure. PCA was used to give a representative map of the different areas.
Results
Effect of exercise training and dietary lipid content on the growth, organ mass, flesh composition and hydrolyzed amino acid compositions of gibel carp

Influences of aerobic exercise train and dietary lipid content on growth, organ mass, flesh composition and textural properties of gibel carp. (A) Weight gain rate (%); (B) Hepatosomatic index (HSI); The basic composition of flesh is shown in Panels C-G. (C) Moisture (%); (D) Protein content (%); (E) Fat content (%); (F) Ash content (%); (G) Glycogen content (mg/g); Panels H:O represent muscular textural properties. (H) Centrifugal water loss (%); (I) Springiness (%); (J) Hardness (g); (K) Fracturability (g/sec); (L) Flexibility (mm); (M) Stickiness (g); (N) Adhesiveness (g.sec); (O) Toughness (g.sec). Columns represent the mean +- SEM (n = 6). Two-way ANOVA P values are shown in each panel, in which "Train" represents the effects of exercise training, "Diet" represents the effects of dietary lipid content, and "Train x Diet" represents the interaction between exercise training and dietary lipid content. Once interactions were identified, different lowercase letters (a, b, or c) were used to represent significant differences among all groups (P < 0.05). The uppercase letters A and B represent significant differences between groups with exercise training or without exercise training on the medium-fat diet (P < 0.05). The uppercase letters X and Y represent significant differences between groups with exercise training or without exercise training on the high-fat diet (P < 0.05). Means with * are significantly different between groups with the same dietary fat content diets at exercise training or without exercise training (P < 0.05).

As displayed in Fig. 1A, ET significantly reduced the weight gain rate of fish regardless of dietary fat content. HFD significantly increased the weight gain rate whether fish received ET or not. The hepatosomatic index (HSI) in the HFN group was significantly higher than that in the MFN group (Fig. 1B). The flesh proximate compositions are shown in Fig. 1C-G. The moisture in the HFN group was significantly higher than that in the MFN group. Meanwhile, ET significantly increased the moisture when fish were fed diets with high fat content (Fig. 1C). The ash content in the HFT group was significantly lower than that in the MFT group (Fig. 1F). The ET and HFD treatments interacted to affect the protein and fat content in the flesh, which in the HFN group significantly increased compared to that in the MFN group (Fig. 1D, E). ET and HFD significantly increased the glycogen content in flesh (Fig. 1G). The hydrolyzed amino acid compositions of flesh are shown in Table S5. There was an interaction between ET and dietary fat content in the contents of lysine, arginine, leucine, isoleucine, glycine, and essential amino acid (EAA) in flesh. The lysine, arginine and isoleucine contents in the MFN groups were significantly lower than those in the other groups. The leucine, valine and EAA contents in the HFD groups were significantly higher those in the MFD groups. HFD significantly increased the levels of methionine, phenylalanine, aspartic acid, glutamic acid, alanine and nonessential amino acid (NEAA). Meanwhile, HFD significantly increased tyrosine content whether fish received ET or not.
Effect of exercise training and dietary lipid content on flesh textural properties and histological analysis of gibel carp

The flesh texture measurement data are presented in Fig. 1H-O. ET significantly increased the hardness and fracturability and decreased the centrifugal water loss of flesh, irrespective of the dietary fat content (Fig. 1H, J, M). HFD significantly decreased the hardness and increased the stickiness whether fish received ET or not (Fig. 1J, K). ET significantly increased the flexibility when fish were fed a medium-fat diet (Fig. 1L). HFD significantly decreased the flexibility and increased the fracturability of flesh when fish received ET (Fig. 1L, M). The ET and HFD treatments interacted to affect the springiness and adhesiveness in the flesh. The springiness in the MFN group was significantly lower than that in the other groups and the adhesiveness in the MFT group was significantly increased compared that in the other groups (Fig. 1I, N). To further explore the effects of ET and dietary fat content on volatile compounds in flesh, a metabolomics analysis based on GC/MS was conducted to evaluate the volatile metabolites. A total of 86 volatile metabolites were identified in muscle, including esters (31), alkanes (16), ketones (9), alcohols (5), alkenes (4), aldehydes (3), amines (3) and others (15) (Fig. 5A) (Table S8). The relative area of the individual was subjected to a one-way ANOVA. Compared with the MFN group, 32 volatile metabolites showed significant changes in the HFT group (P value threshold: 0.05) (Fig. 5B) (Table S9). The principal component analysis (PCA) score plot is shown in Fig. 5C. The MFN group and MFT were completely separated from the other groups. The results of PCA indicated that HFD and ET both significantly affected the muscle volatile metabolites. The heatmap with 50 volatile metabolites was generated using MetaboAnalyst 5.0 software; thus, the changes in the altered metabolite levels that were caused by the dietary fat content and ET were intuitively identified (Fig. 5D).

Metabolomics analysis was used to investigate the specific mechanism of the effects of ET and dietary fat content on nonvolatile metabolites in flesh. The identified metabolites were enriched in specific pathways based on the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database. The specific pathways in the flesh of fish fed MFD affected by ET are shown in Fig. 6A. Alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism, pyruvate metabolism, citrate cycle and purine metabolism were identified as the main impacted pathways in muscle affected by ET. The specific pathways in the flesh of fish not receiving ET affected by HFD are shown in Fig. 6B. Amino sugar and nucleotide sugar metabolism, fatty acid elongation, fatty acid degradation, starch and sucrose metabolism and the citrate cycle were identified as the main impacted pathways in muscle affected by HFD. Fig. 6C presents the specific pathways in the flesh of fish fed a HFD affected by ET. Butanoate metabolism, purine metabolism, valine, leucine and isoleucine degradation and glutamine and glutamate metabolism were identified as the main impacted pathways in muscle. The principal component analysis (PCA) score plot is shown in Fig. 6D. Part of the overlap appeared within the control groups and experimental groups. However, HFT had the least overlap with the control, followed by MFT. Based on the content changes of differential metabolites of flesh and the reported pathways from the KEGG database, the main pathways of flesh metabolism affected by ET and HFD were obtained (Fig. 6E).
Discussion

Increased body fat levels due to excessive energy intake had negative impacts on flesh quality and liver health, and ET could improve liver health and muscle flavour by burning this energy. When energy intake exceeds energy expenditure, redundant energy is stored, as evidenced by the weight gain rate, while ET continuously mobilizes energy to sustain the body's activities. In the present study, the HFD increased the weight gain rate, while ET consumed more energy and reduced the weight gain rate. The results were as expected. Furthermore, ET was observed to reduce the high HSI of gibel carp induced by the HFD. HFD easily causes fatty liver in farmed fish species, and a high HSI is an important phenotype of fatty liver. Studies in this experiment have indicated that appropriate ET can promote liver health in farmed fish. The nutrient composition can partly reflect flesh quality. Protein, lipid and glycogen contents are vital nutrients of fish flesh. In this study, HFD elevated the content of muscle fat and glycogen, and ET reduced muscle fat and increased the glycogen content, which is consistent with the studies by. The results indicated that excessive fat intake is stored as muscular fat, while more fat is broken down to provide the energy necessary for ET. ET increased the muscle glycogen content, which may be a way for experienced fish to expand their energy reserves to adapt to exercise training. This was confirmed by the results of the sections stained for glycogen in muscle. Many of the aroma compounds in flesh originate from the breakdown of sugars. The increased glycogen content may help to improve the flavour of flesh quality.

ET has a direct effect on the muscle of fish, and this study found that ET improved flesh quality by changing the physicochemical properties of muscle. Muscular texture is strongly associated with consumer acceptance, and soft fillets are less accepted by consumers. This study found that the hardness, flexibility and adhesiveness were decreased in the fish fed a HFD. However, the fish that received ET appeared to have higher levels of hardness and fracturability in flesh, which alleviated the negative effects of HFD on flesh texture. The muscle fat content is closely related to flesh texture. The above result agreed with the trend of muscle fat content, which indicated that ET-increased flesh hardness might be partially related to the reduced muscle fat content. Some studies have shown that training results in an increase in muscle fiber density and a change in muscle fiber diameter. This phenomenon was also found in this study, in which ET increased the density and diameter of myofibers. Myofiber characteristics are a main determinant of texture. In this study, ET increased the muscular water holding capacity (decreased the centrifugal water loss), firmness (hardness) and stickiness, suggesting that a higher density and diameter of muscle fiber resulted in a better texture of flesh. Collagen content is closely connected with meat texture. ET increased the muscle collagen content in this study, which could partially explain the improvement in water holding capacity and firmness. Overall, ET improves fish texture and contributes to providing consumers with better-tasting aquatic products.

Flavour nucleotides and flavour amino acids are vital contributors to the taste of aquatic products. This study showed that both ET and HFD increased the IMP content in muscle. Accumulating evidence indicates that exercise training increases the level of IMP in fish flesh. However, few studies have reported on its specific mechanisms. Purine metabolism is the main pathway for IMP synthesis. Metabolomics revealed that ET and HFD significantly affected the purine metabolism pathway. The HPLC results showed that ET and HFD resulted in a large change in purine metabolites such as inosine, hypoxanthine and AMP, suggesting that the deposition of IMP in flesh may partly be associated with the purine metabolism pathway. IMP makes a great contribution to the umami of meat products, and the flavour of food is improved effectively via the accumulation of IMP in flesh. The present study partly indicated that the purine metabolic pathway affecting IMP deposition contributes to improving the taste of cultured fish.

Free amino acids are another important contributor to the muscle flavour of fish products. This study found that ET decreased the FAA content including umami and sweet amino acids, which will reduce consumer acceptance of flesh to a certain extent. A previous study also found that high-intensity exercise has a negative impact on muscle amino acid composition. This may be because fish need to consume more amino acids to provide energy during ET, resulting in less FAA deposition in muscle. The metabolomics results also agreed with this finding. However, feeding HFD to experimental fish during exercise restored FAA contents in flesh. This may be related to the fact that the intake of HFD increased the body's energy reserves and conserves FAA in flesh, which needs to be confirmed by further research. Currently, it is becoming common to treat premarket farmed fish with in-water exercise without feeding to improve muscle quality. The current results imply that this approach is detrimental to the deposition of flavour amino acids in flesh. This can be mitigated by appropriate feeding of HFD.

The fatty acid compositions in flesh reflect the healthcare conditions and nutritive values. The current study found that ET and HFD were able to increase the n-3 PUFA, n-6 PUFA and HUFA levels. Moreover, the combined action of ET and HFD was more effective in enhancing n-3 HUFA, n-6 HUFA and HUFA levels in flesh compared to the effects of ET and HFD alone. This phenomenon may be associated with fatty acid redeployment and the preference of SFA for energy provision during ET. EPA and DHA cannot be synthesized by humans and are only obtained from food, which is indispensable for the growth and development of humans and animals. This experiment found that ET and HFD increased the DHA content and that the combined effect was better. These results demonstrated that ET and HFD in combination is considered a potential method to regulate the nutritional value of fatty acids in fillets.

Combined E-nose and GC/MS analysis reveals the effect of ET and dietary fat content on muscle volatile compounds. The E-nose was able to successfully distinguish between the muscles of crabs farmed in different patterns. In this study, the results of PCA plots clearly demonstrated that both ET and dietary fat level have an impact on volatile compounds. GC/MS was used to further investigate the specific effects of HFD and ET on muscle volatile compounds. In the GC/MS analysis, a total of 32 metabolites were calculated to obtain biomarkers that contributed to distinguishing the metabolic profiles among all treatments. The relative hexadecenoic acid, ethyl ester and methyl stearate contents were increased in the HFT group. Hexadecanoic acid, ethyl ester contains a creamy and slightly waxy aroma. Methyl stearate gives off a honey-like and iris-like aroma. Therefore, the present study showed that the combined effect of ET and HFD may enhance the aroma of fish flesh by altering some volatile compounds with fragrance. The experimental fish absorbed amino acids, fatty acids and carbohydrates from the diet, which were oxidized and broken down in the muscle to meet the high demand for energy during the swimming exercise. Furthermore, they are the main precursors to volatile compounds in the flesh, which may be responsible for the change in certain volatile compounds in muscle. Similar results were found in largemouth bass (Micropterus salmoides) in which the contents of carboxylic acids, esters and aromatic compounds and smethyl sulfate in muscle were increased after swimming exercise. In conclusion, the analysis of E-nose and GC/MS illustrated that the combination of ET and HFD could improve the flavour of flesh by enhancing the levels of some aroma volatile compounds.
Conclusions

In conclusion, HFD reduced flesh hardness, flexibility and adhesiveness related to an increased muscle fat content. However, ET improved flesh texture by reducing muscle fat content and increasing the density and diameter of myofibers. ET decreased the muscular umami and sweet amino acid contents, but HFD feeding reversed this negative effect. Moreover, the combination of ET and HFD enhanced the contents of umami nucleotides and EPA. Metabolomics analysis revealed that the alanine, aspartate and glutamate metabolism and the citrate cycle and purine metabolism are the main pathways affected by ET and HFD. Furthermore, the combination of ET and HFD could improve the flavour of flesh by enhancing the levels of some aroma volatile compounds. The combination of ET and HFD is a new strategy for improving the quality of fish and providing healthier and more delectable aquatic products for humans.

We have generated an iPSCs line (CTGUi001-A) from dermal fibroblasts of a 16-year-old male Fabry disease patient with a novel GLA gene mutation (c.156C > A) using Sendai virus encoding the four Yamanaka factors OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and c-MYC. passages.text: Prevalence of Fabry Disease in patients with left ventricular hypertrophy in Turkey: Multicenter study (LVH-TR subgroup analysis).

PURPOSE: In this prospective study we aimed to determine the rate of Fabry Disease (FD) in patients with left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), and to evaluate the clinical presentations of patients with FD in a comprehensive manner. In addition, we aimed to raise awareness about this issue by allowing early diagnosis and treatment of FD. METHODS: Our study was planned as national, multicenter, observational. Totally 22 different centers participated in this study. A total of 886 patients diagnosed with LVH by echocardiography (ECHO) were included in the study. Demographic data, biochemical parameters, electrocardiography (ECG) findings, ECHO findings, treatments and clinical findings of the patients were recorded. Dry blood samples were sent from male patients with suspected FD. The alpha-Gal A enzyme level was checked and genetic testing was performed in patients with low enzyme levels. Female patients suspected of FD were genetically tested with the GLA Gene Mutation Analysis. RESULTS: FD was suspected in a total of 143 (16.13%) patients included in the study. The alpha-Gal-A enzyme level was found to be low in 43 (4.85%) patients whom enzyme testing was requested. GLA gene mutation analysis was positive in 14 (1.58%) patients. Male gender, E/e' mean ,and severe hypertrophy are important risk factor for FD. CONCLUSION: In daily cardiology practice, FD should be kept in mind not only in adult patients with unexplained LVH but also in the entire LVH population. Dry blood test (DBS) should be considered in high-risk patients, and mutation analysis should be considered in required patients.

passages.text: MDU-Net: multi-scale densely connected U-Net for biomedical image segmentation.

Biomedical image segmentation plays a central role in quantitative analysis, clinical diagnosis, and medical intervention. In the light of the fully convolutional networks (FCN) and U-Net, deep convolutional networks (DNNs) have made significant contributions to biomedical image segmentation applications. In this paper, we propose three different multi-scale dense connections (MDC) for the encoder, the decoder of U-shaped architectures, and across them. Based on three dense connections, we propose a multi-scale densely connected U-Net (MDU-Net) for biomedical image segmentation. MDU-Net directly fuses the neighboring feature maps with different scales from both higher layers and lower layers to strengthen feature propagation in the current layer. Multi-scale dense connections, which contain shorter connections between layers close to the input and output, also make a much deeper U-Net possible. Besides, we introduce quantization to alleviate the potential overfitting in dense connections, and further improve the segmentation performance. We evaluate our proposed model on the MICCAI 2015 Gland Segmentation (GlaS) dataset. The three MDC improve U-Net performance by up to 1.8% on test A and 3.5% on test B in the MICCAI Gland dataset. Meanwhile, the MDU-Net with quantization obviously improves the segmentation performance of original U-Net.
Monitoring prothrombin activation in plasma through loss of Forster resonance energy transfer.

BACKGROUND: Current assays that monitor thrombin generation in plasma rely on fluorogenic substrates to follow the kinetics of zymogen activation, which may be complicated by substrate cleavage from other proteases. In addition, these assays depend on activation following cleavage at the prothrombin R320 site and fail to report the cleavage at the alternative R271 site, leading to the shedding of the auxiliary Gla and kringle domains of prothrombin. OBJECTIVES: To develop a plasma assay that directly monitors prothrombin activation independent of fluorogenic substrate hydrolysis. METHODS: Cleavage at the R271 site of prothrombin is monitored through loss of Forster resonance energy transfer in plasma coagulated along the extrinsic or intrinsic pathway. RESULTS: The availability of factor (F)V in plasma strongly influences the rate of prothrombin activation. The rate of thrombin formation is equally perturbed in FV or prothrombin-depleted plasma, implicating that the thrombin-catalyzed feedback reactions that amplify the coagulation response play an important role in generating sufficient amounts of FVa required for the assembly of prothrombinase. Congenital deficiencies in FVIII and FIX significantly slow down cleavage at R271 in plasma coagulated along the extrinsic and intrinsic pathways. Prothrombin activation in FXI-deficient plasma is only perturbed when coagulation is triggered along the intrinsic pathway. CONCLUSION: The Forster resonance energy transfer assay enables direct monitoring of prothrombin activation through cleavage at R271 without the need for fluorogenic substrates. The assay is sensitive enough to assess how deficiencies in coagulation factors affect thrombin formation.

passages.text: MESTrans: Multi-scale embedding spatial transformer for medical image segmentation.

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Transformers profiting from global information modeling derived from the self-attention mechanism have recently achieved remarkable performance in computer vision. In this study, a novel transformer-based medical image segmentation network called the multi-scale embedding spatial transformer (MESTrans) was proposed for medical image segmentation. METHODS: First, a dataset called COVID-DS36 was created from 4369 computed tomography (CT) images of 36 patients from a partner hospital, of which 18 had COVID-19 and 18 did not. Subsequently, a novel medical image segmentation network was proposed, which introduced a self-attention mechanism to improve the inherent limitation of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and was capable of adaptively extracting discriminative information in both global and local content. Specifically, based on U-Net, a multi-scale embedding block (MEB) and multi-layer spatial attention transformer (SATrans) structure were designed, which can dynamically adjust the receptive field in accordance with the input content. The spatial relationship between multi-level and multi-scale image patches was modeled, and the global context information was captured effectively. To make the network concentrate on the salient feature region, a feature fusion module (FFM) was established, which performed global learning and soft selection between shallow and deep features, adaptively combining the encoder and decoder features. Four datasets comprising CT images, magnetic resonance (MR) images, and H&E-stained slide images were used to assess the performance of the proposed network. RESULTS: Experiments were performed using four different types of medical image datasets. For the COVID-DS36 dataset, our method achieved a Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 81.23%. For the GlaS dataset, 89.95% DSC and 82.39% intersection over union (IoU) were obtained. On the Synapse dataset, the average DSC was 77.48% and the average Hausdorff distance (HD) was 31.69 mm. For the I2CVB dataset, 92.3% DSC and 85.8% IoU were obtained. CONCLUSIONS: The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model has an excellent generalization ability and outperforms other state-of-the-art methods. It is expected to be a potent tool to assist clinicians in auxiliary diagnosis and to promote the development of medical intelligence technology.
